entity.name: MapSmith
entity.description: Maintainer of MapSmith, an open-source MCP server that gives AI agents professional GIS geoprocessing with verifiable provenance. Work is unfunded to date: 16 semantic tools, 336 closed-form tests and a 375-run published benchmark were built without external support.

projects.name: MapSmith
projects.description: An MCP server for professional GIS geoprocessing — buffers, overlays, reprojections, zonal statistics, terrain and hydrology — where every output carries a provenance manifest: input checksums, exact parameters, motivated CRS decisions, engine versions, and the verification checks that ran. Geometry and numbers always come from engine executions, never from a language model. The aim is that an analysis produced by an agent can be defended afterwards, by someone who was not there when it ran.

channels.description: Written contact for funders. Arrangements are agreed in writing; no payment provider is published here.

plans.name: A correctness suite for geospatial AI
plans.description: Existing GIS agent benchmarks measure whether a task completed, not whether the number that came out is true — several of them say so themselves, because they have no ground-truth outputs. This plan funds a public suite of traps with hand-computable answers (undetected CRS mismatch, feet read as metres, an unset TIFF predictor producing plausible terrain), a runner, a two-number score, and a clean set so that refusing everything cannot score well.

plans.name: An open specification for the provenance manifest
plans.description: The manifest is useful to others only if it is a format rather than a feature. This plan funds a standalone specification with a versioned JSON Schema, a conformance suite of manifests that must validate and must be rejected, and a reference emitter of about a hundred lines that does not import MapSmith — so that any tool can produce one.

plans.name: Ongoing maintenance
plans.description: Security fixes, engine upgrades, and keeping the published benchmark honest — including republishing results that contradict earlier conclusions, which has already happened once.
